changes.new:
### Why the metrics select different numbers of clusters

The MOOC experiment uses 1,250 Wikinews articles with five editorial
categories: business, entertainment, sport, politics and tech.
`StringEncoder` converts the texts into numerical features; k-means then
groups those vectors without using the category labels during its fit.
V-measure and ARI compare the resulting groups with the editorial categories.
Silhouette instead evaluates distances within and between the predicted
groups. These criteria need not select the same partition.

![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/classical-ml-clustering/mooc-news-external-metrics.png|Original MOOC V-measure and ARI curves for Wikinews clustering]]

*scikit-learn MOOC authors,
[Clustering performance metrics in the presence of labels](https://inria.github.io/scikit-learn-mooc/python_scripts/clustering_supervised_metrics.html),
CC BY 4.0. Complete original figure, unchanged. Blue and orange curves show
training and validation scores across five `ShuffleSplit` partitions with
75% used for fitting k-means. The error bars describe variation across these
partitions, not a confidence interval.*

Among the tested values from 2 through 10, both external metrics reach their
largest mean near 7. Their values remain far below 1: the seven groups do
not exactly reproduce the five editorial categories. Nor does this result
establish that there are seven underlying topics. It identifies a useful
candidate under two specified agreement criteria and one text representation.

In the source code, `StringEncoder` is fitted once on all articles before
these splits. The curves therefore compare k-means fits within that fixed
representation. They are not a held-out evaluation of the complete
text-encoding-and-clustering pipeline. To evaluate the whole procedure on
new articles, refit the encoder inside each training partition as well.

![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/classical-ml-clustering/mooc-news-silhouette.png|Original MOOC silhouette curves for the same news representation]]

*scikit-learn MOOC authors,
[Clustering performance metrics in the presence of labels](https://inria.github.io/scikit-learn-mooc/python_scripts/clustering_supervised_metrics.html),
CC BY 4.0. Complete original figure, unchanged. Each pale line uses a different
half-sample for fitting and predicts the other half; the black line is their
mean over ten splits. These split sizes differ from the preceding experiment.
The encoder is again fixed before splitting.*

The silhouette analysis tests 2–10 clusters and then 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 and 70.
Its mean reaches a maximum near 30, at only about 0.16. For these vectors,
the smaller groups give a better balance of within-group and between-group
distances. The peak does not prove that every small group
has a distinct editorial meaning, and adding further clusters does not keep
improving the score.

> However, categorizing news articles in too fine-grained topics would make the
> navigation on a news website too confusing. Therefore for this application, it
> can be meaningful to select a number of clusters that is smaller than the
> number of clusters which maximizes the silhouette score.

*scikit-learn MOOC authors, same lesson, CC BY 4.0.
Original English excerpt; not translated.*

If the objective is to reproduce those five categories, the category labels
can instead train a supervised classifier. If the objective is to find
alternative groupings, inspect representative articles, mixed-topic articles
and the proposed navigation before selecting a number of groups. Once
editorial labels or downstream outcomes influence that choice, they are part
of model selection; an independent assessment needs separate data.

## Устойчивость

### Quantile preprocessing and discrete layers

The MOOC's customer-segmentation exercise uses three RFM features:
recency, frequency and monetary value. It repeatedly clusters half-samples
of a 2,000-customer dataset, comparing `StandardScaler` with
`QuantileTransformer`. Both runs use five initializations of k-means.
In that experiment the quantile transformation makes the silhouette curves
somewhat more stable, but the scores remain low. The illustrated six-cluster
partition below is a further inspection of the full dataset, not the value
that maximized silhouette in every half-sample.

![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/classical-ml-clustering/mooc-rfm-quantile-layers.png|Original MOOC customer clusters in quantile-transformed RFM space]]

*scikit-learn MOOC authors,
[Solution for Exercise M4.01, Stability of k-means](https://inria.github.io/scikit-learn-mooc/python_scripts/clustering_sol_01.html),
CC BY 4.0. Complete original figure, unchanged. All three axes are transformed
feature values, not days, purchase counts or money. Colours denote the six
k-means groups; the planes at repeated frequency values are a property of
the data and transformation, not six independently established customer types.*

> We can observe that the quantile-transformed data has a structure of layered
> planes because of the discrete integer levels for the lowest values of the
> "Frequency" feature which are overrepresented in the dataset.

*scikit-learn MOOC authors, same solution, CC BY 4.0.
Original English source comment, presented as prose without translation.*

A quantile transformer estimates each feature's distribution from training
values and maps its quantiles to a chosen output distribution. With uniform
output, feature values become positions between 0 and 1. This is nonlinear:
equal differences in purchase counts need not remain equal distances.
Repeated input values receive the same transformed value. A discrete
frequency feature therefore retains repeated coordinate levels; the
transformation does not turn it into a continuous distribution.

For five counts $(0,1,1,2,100)$ and five quantiles, the fitted training
quantiles are those same sorted values. Their uniform reference positions
are $(0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1)$. Scikit-learn symmetrically interpolates repeated
interior values: each occurrence of 1 receives the middle position 0.375.
The transformed values are consequently $(0,0.375,0.375,0.75,1)$.
The original gap from 1 to 2 was 1 and becomes 0.375; the gap from 2 to 100
was 98 and becomes 0.25. K-means now optimizes distances in this changed
geometry. None of these steps establishes that either gap separates
meaningful customer groups.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import QuantileTransformer

purchase_counts = np.array([0., 1., 1., 2., 100.])[:, None]
quantile_map = QuantileTransformer(
    n_quantiles=5, output_distribution="uniform", random_state=0,
)
count_positions = quantile_map.fit_transform(purchase_counts).ravel()
np.testing.assert_allclose(count_positions, [0., .375, .375, .75, 1.])
np.testing.assert_allclose(quantile_map.inverse_transform(
    count_positions[:, None]
), purchase_counts)
print("Transformed counts:", count_positions)
```

Changing rubles to thousands of rubles leaves the earlier standardized
distances unchanged. Quantile preprocessing changes relative distances.
Its stability should therefore be assessed together with the
resulting customer profiles, not by comparing silhouette values alone across
different transformed spaces. The source's layered plot is a reason to
inspect the frequency distribution and the other two features, rather than
to interpret every coloured region as a customer segment. Transformation
details are documented in
[scikit-learn, QuantileTransformer](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.preprocessing.QuantileTransformer.html).

## Кластеризация как построение признаков

supplementary: Complete archived hdbscan-how.rst, 403 lines: core distances, mutual reachability, MST, component hierarchy, condensation, EOM, membership strength.

Complete scikit-learn 1.9.1 QuantileTransformer._transform_col implementation, fetched from the release tag; current KMeans/HDBSCAN/QuantileTransformer API pages located and compared with actual CPU behavior. Not a complete read of all API navigation or guide pages.
exclusions: K-means optimizes squared distances, not an unsquared-distance objective; initialization/restarts do not guarantee a global optimum.
The MOOC transformer paragraph says nearest centroid, but KMeans.transform returns distances to every centroid; the current complete nonlinear feature example preserves the correct contract.

Source external-metric curves fit StringEncoder on all texts before CV: they evaluate KMeans within a fixed representation, not the full pipeline. The silhouette experiment uses different splits; no independent full-pipeline estimate inferred.
Source silhouette peaks are dataset/representation-dependent, not proof of seven or thirty true topics. No universal monotonic test-quality or cluster-count claim imported.
Noise label -1 is not a cluster count; sklearn and contrib HDBSCAN neighbor conventions differ.
Quantile maps preserve repeated feature values; prettier or more stable plots do not establish useful customer segments. No source-wide California Housing/RFM/Wikinews rerun claimed.

An initial six-observation quantile toy exhibited floating percentile tie shifts; it was replaced with an exactly representable five-quantile example and checked against the released interpolation code, without loosening tolerances.
